The People Who Shape Our Careers

Oct 17, 2017 • Janice Cotcher

I previously wrote about My Grandmother, the Teacher

At the end of Grade 10, I wanted to be an accountant. At the end of Grade 11, I wanted to be a math teacher. Throughout Grade 12, my experiences confirmed that I was passionate about education.

One of my high school math teachers was one of the kindest, more interesting people I’ve ever met. Every student felt included and cared for. Every student was encouraged to do better regardless of ability. My Grade 8 teacher did us a disservice by only covering a tenth of the curriculum. As a result, I failed my first Grade 9 Algebra test because I lacked the prerequisite information. It was the only time in my life that I was blissfully unaware of my performance on an assessment. I was absolutely devastated. My teacher knew I was upset. He quietly took me aside, and I told me that I had to ability to catch up and excel in the course. On one occasion, I inadvertently overheard my teacher asking a pregnant student how he can help her succeed. He performed his acts of generosity quietly. He inspired me to invoke changes in and out of the classroom.

As a first year teacher, my supervising superintendent served as my unofficial mentor. I was part of a mentorship program for beginning teachers, but my assigned mentor was wholly unsuited (a story for another time). The superintendent was one of the few people I knew in the school division before I began my position. He was a master’s student while I was working on my BEd and often assisted my peers and me with integrating technology in the classroom. After getting my contact information from my faculty advisor, he encouraged me to apply for a math/technology in his division.

Throughout the school year, it was nice to have a mentor that really got me. He helped me with long-range planning and taught me how to prepare for when a lesson doesn’t work out. The thing that stuck with me the most was when he admitted, “Everyone, at least once, has walked into the classroom not knowing what they were going to do.” It might sound like a terrible thing to be unprepared for a lesson.  At the time, I was a technology teacher with a computer lab filled with ancient computers. Some days the network didn’t work*. Some days the internet didn’t work. Sometimes programs stopped working.  My plans didn’t always work because of limited or no resources.  His advice was meaningful to me at the time. Plans don’t always work and you have to adapt quickly.

Before I began teaching, I didn’t realize the difference administrators make on the school’s culture. I had an excellent school and division administrators during my first teaching position. Due to my inexperience, I assumed that this was the norm. My most recent principal is the probably the most positive educator I’ve ever met. Each staff meeting began with celebrations of accomplishments and showing appreciation for the work of the staff. It was a big cultural shift that I needed. Too often in the past, I only ever heard from administrators when something was wrong. Teaching can be a thankless job, but school staff can encourage and show thankfulness to each other.

*Sometime I’ll tell the story about the time our server was down for a month.
